source.title_on_document: What Does AI Do for Cultural Interpretation? A Randomized Experiment on Close Reading Poems with Exposure to AI Interpretation

supplement.where: "Supplementary Materials" cited throughout (B.1, B.2, B.3, B.4, B.8); data, analysis, and interface code at https://closereading-ai.app (p. 2, footnote 2). Appendix A in this PDF holds only Tables 7 and 8 (p. 18).
supplement.holds: Survey questions (B.1), task questions (B.2), poem texts (B.3), scoring rubrics (B.4), AI responses and prompts (B.8), and exploratory analyses adjusting for number of AI interpretations viewed (B.1, cited p. 9). The main effect estimates (Table 1) and subgroup tables (Tables 7, 8) are in this PDF.

paper_design_summary: Preregistered between-subjects online experiment with 400 US Prolific participants (lay readers), randomly assigned to close-read three poems with no AI help (Control, n = 141), with one GPT-4o interpretation shown beneath the poem (AI-Single, n = 115), or with three stacked GPT-4o interpretations (AI-Multiple, n = 144). For each poem participants identified three stylistic features and explained their effects; two English-trained graders scored Feature Identification (0/1), Interpretation Quality (1-5), and Writing Quality (1-5). Participants also self-rated appreciation, enjoyment, and self-efficacy (7-point scales). No outcome measures creativity, novelty, or diversity across people.

studies.label: Main experiment (close reading of three poems, Control vs AI-Single vs AI-Multiple)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: no AI interpretation (Control), one pre-generated AI interpretation (AI-Single), or three pre-generated AI interpretations (AI-Multiple); same condition for all three poems; poem order also randomized
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Close reading a poem without assistance

arms.name: AI-Single
arms.description: Close reading a poem while one GPT-4o interpretation is displayed beneath the poem by default

arms.name: AI-Multiple
arms.description: Close reading a poem with three GPT-4o interpretations stacked; one visible by default, two more behind labeled buttons

participants.exclusions: 405 recruited from Prolific; 400 remain "after excluding those who completed any of the poems in excessively short time (3 SDs below the mean)" (5 excluded). Per-arm counts at assignment are not given. A chi-squared test on the arm sizes was not significant (chi2(2) = 3.815, p = 0.149).
participants.who: Prolific crowdworkers with 100% approval rate, based in the US, English as primary language and fluent; 51.6% had taken at least one college-level humanities course (classed as experienced readers), 48.4% inexperienced
participants.quote: Our randomized experiment yielded 400 participants in all: 141 in the Control, 115 in the AI-Single, and 144 in the AI-Multiple.

ai_tool.how_used: Researchers prompted GPT-4o with the same task instructions given to participants and displayed the resulting interpretation(s) beside the participant's answer fields; no live chat. AI-Multiple showed three distinct interpretations, each identifying different stylistic features. Self-reported non-use: 54.8% of instances in AI-Single and 47.0% in AI-Multiple (p. 2; Table 4, p. 12).

task.description: Close reading (literary interpretation) of three poems (Pastan "Love Poem", Nelson "Dusting", Hughes "Theme for English B"), adapted from the Critical Reader's Interpretive Toolkit: per poem, identify a distinctive word/phrase, a line revealing voice or perspective, and an element of poetic style, and explain in 2-3 sentences how each contributes to the poem's meaning. Analytical interpretation task, not judged on creativity or novelty.
task.duration: Whole study about one hour (p. 6, Section 3.3)

outcomes.name: Interpretation Quality
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Depth and insight of the explanation, 1-5 rubric (1 = poor, 3 = average, 5 = excellent), scored by two trained graders (undergraduate degrees in English, one a PhD student in English); averaged over the three tasks per poem; ICC(2,1) = 0.76 on a 70-participant validation set (pp. 5-6). Construct is interpretive quality of a close reading, not creativity; AI was available when produced, so it would be with_ai only if close reading counted as a creative task.

contrasts.reported: Mixed-effects coefficient 0.865*** [0.664, 1.065], p < 0.001 (Table 1). Instance-level means: AI-Single 2.52 (0.95) vs Control 1.65 (0.75) (Table 3). Participant-level by expertise (Table 7): inexperienced Control 1.617 (0.810) vs AI-Single 2.564 (0.912), d = 1.106, adj. p = 0.000; experienced Control 1.684 (0.553) vs AI-Single 2.474 (0.797), d = 1.166, adj. p = 0.000.

company_involvement.description: Funded by SSHRC Insight Development Grant 430-2024-00336; authors at University of Chicago and Duke. GPT-4o (OpenAI) used as a tool only.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to generative-AI interpretations (p. 4) and 400 people were analyzed (p. 6), but the task is analytical close reading of poems and the outputs are scored for feature-identification correctness, interpretation quality (depth and insight), and writing quality, not for creativity, novelty, or diversity across people. The remaining outcomes are self-reported (appreciation, enjoyment, self-efficacy). The only similarity measure is overlap between each participant's answer and the AI text, described for AI arms only, not diversity across people. Criterion 1 is met only in the sense of random assignment to AI; the task is arguably not a creative or ideation task under codebook Section 1.

one_line_finding: Seeing one GPT-4o interpretation raised graded Interpretation Quality by 0.865 points (95% CI [0.664, 1.065]) and Writing Quality by 1.035 points on 1-5 scales versus no AI, and three interpretations raised them by 0.593 and 0.784 (Table 1, p. 7), but none of these outcomes measures creativity or diversity.
open_questions: Whether close reading (interpretation with multiple acceptable readings) should count as a creative task under codebook Section 1; I coded it out because outputs are graded for correctness and interpretive quality, not novelty or originality.
Per-arm counts at assignment (before the 5 exclusions) are not reported.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reported, not scored on the output: Appreciation, Enjoyment, Self-efficacy (mixed-effects ordinal log-odds, Table 2, p. 9: AI-Single 0.899***, 0.969***, 0.900**; AI-Multiple -0.070, -0.248, -0.352, all ns; subgroup Mann-Whitney tests in Table 8, p. 18). Descriptive, non-randomized analyses also not listed: viewing behavior in AI-Multiple (Table 3, p. 11: 42.1% viewed one, 12.3% two, 45.6% three), cursor time allocation (Figure 5, p. 11), self-reported AI use (Tables 4 and 5, p. 12), and textual overlap/copy rate between participant answers and AI text (Section 5.4, Table 6, p. 13). Table 1 regressions are mixed-effects linear models with condition, expertise, poem type, and poem position as fixed effects and a participant random effect (p. 6, Section 3.4.2); one observation per participant-poem (423 + 345 + 432 = 1200 instances, p. 6). Table 7 subgroup statistics are participant-level averages with Mann-Whitney U tests and Holm-Bonferroni adjusted p-values; subgroup ns are not printed. AI benchmark scores under the same rubric: Feature 1.00, Interpretation 4.00, Writing 4.07 (p. 13). Pilots (n = 20, 60, 90, 100) were used to refine instructions only (p. 4).
